title: Tests On Von Mises Distributions
notes: Open with the chapter purpose: after learning uniformity and goodness-of-fit, we now assume a von Mises working model and ask parameter questions. Emphasize that the deck follows the notebook rather than reproducing tables: every test is expressed through resultants, fitted concentration, and calibration checks.

title: A Decision Route, Not A Test Catalog
notes: Use the route map to orient students. The sequence is not a list of tests; it is a decision workflow. First read the sample resultant, then test one mean direction, compare two or more groups, check common concentration, and finally challenge the von Mises assumption.

title: The Von Mises Working Model
notes: Explain the von Mises model as the circular analogue of a normal model with mean direction and concentration. The important point for inference is that all likelihood information flows through C, S, and R, so geometry and statistics are the same object here.

title: The Resultant Is The Sufficient Dashboard
notes: Spend time on the resultant diagram. Each observation contributes a unit vector, the vector sum points to the estimated mean direction, and its length reports concentration. Short resultants mean either diffuse data or competing modes, so no mean-direction test should be interpreted without this diagnostic.

title: One-Sample Null: Rotate To The Proposed Mean
notes: Present the one-sample test by rotating the hypothesized mean direction to zero. Under the null, sine components should balance above and below the axis. A persistent perpendicular imbalance is the visual signal that the proposed mean direction is misaligned.

title: Confidence Arcs Invert The Test
notes: Frame the confidence arc as an inverse test. Instead of asking whether one mu0 is plausible, sweep candidate directions and retain the ones whose rotated sine imbalance is small enough. Higher kappa or larger n narrows the arc; low concentration makes the arc honestly wide.

title: Profile Likelihood Couples Mean And Concentration
notes: Use the profile likelihood sketch to show why kappa cannot be ignored. For each candidate mean direction, kappa is fitted from the resultant length after rotation. The mean estimate and concentration estimate are coupled, and small samples make that coupling visible.

title: Two Samples: How Much Length Does Pooling Lose?
notes: Move to two samples by drawing separate resultants and the pooled resultant. If the two group means agree, pooling loses little length. If directions separate, the pooled vector is shorter than the sum of separate lengths; that loss is the between-group signal.

title: Watson-Williams As A Resultant Budget
notes: Explain Watson-Williams as circular ANOVA built from resultant budgets. The numerator measures how much resultant length is recovered by allowing group-specific means. The denominator measures within-group circular scatter, and the correction acknowledges finite concentration rather than pretending the circle is a line.

title: Multi-Sample Inference Shares One Concentration
notes: Generalize the geometry to q groups. The slide should make clear that the test is about a common mean direction under a shared concentration assumption, not about arbitrary distributional equality. The center polygon helps students see the between-group component.

title: Check Concentration Homogeneity Before Circular ANOVA
notes: Pause before accepting the ANOVA. Unequal concentration can mimic or hide mean differences because tight groups dominate resultant length. The bootstrap bars in the sketch represent the notebook's habit: test the assumption before trusting the comparison.

title: Von-Misesness Diagnostics Catch Shape Misspecification
notes: Use the second-harmonic diagnostic to catch two-lobed or axial alternatives. A sample can have a stable first resultant and still violate a von Mises shape. Large second-harmonic structure is a warning that the fitted single mode is summarizing the wrong object.

title: P-Values Are Calibrated Geometry
notes: Interpret p-values as calibrated geometry. The observed statistic is a distance or budget loss, and the null distribution tells us how surprising that geometry is after accounting for n and fitted kappa. This is why simulation checks sit beside formulas in the notebook.

title: Applied Lab: Stress-Test The Decision
notes: Present the lab board as a reproducible stress test. Students should vary means, kappas, and sample sizes, then watch when the Watson-Williams decision changes. The goal is not to memorize a p-value; it is to understand which modeling choices drive the decision.

title: Failure Modes And Matching Diagnostics
notes: Make the failure modes explicit. Wrapped normal-looking data, axial mixtures, unequal concentrations, and sparse samples can all produce confident-looking output. The instructor should connect each failure to a diagnostic rather than treating assumptions as boilerplate.

title: Operational Checklist
notes: Close with an operational checklist for inference under von Mises assumptions. Estimate resultants, fit the model, choose the appropriate one-, two-, or multi-sample statistic, verify concentration and shape, then report the decision with the geometric effect that made it happen.
